newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada railways call for end to regulatory barrier.
newsitem.headline: Canada railways call for end to regulatory barrier.

text.p: Canada's two largest railways on Thursday called on the Canadian government to revamp regulations that inhibit efficient grain transportation.

"The current regulations are a barrier to efficient (railcar) allocation. It is designed for 15-car spots at (grain) elevators, not the new 50 to 100 car spots of today," Canadian National Railway Co general manager of grain Phillip Richardson told delegates at the Canada Grains Council meeting in Ottawa.

CN and Canadian Pacific Ltd unit CP Rail System were criticized for rail shipment delays in getting grain to export ports on the Pacific coast. The delays cost the Canadian Wheat Board more than C$20 million in demurrage fines since January.

"Some of this criticism is justified, others are things over which we have little control," Richardson said, citing Rocky Mountain avalanches and land slides that closed CN's mainline twice earlier this year.
"Grain stocks never fell below 420,000 tonnes on the Pacific coast," Richardson added.

A corporate restructuring of CN on Wednesday should help in expediting grain movement to Pacific ports now that locomotive power can be assigned to the Prairie rail fleet by Edmonton, and no longer from Montreal as was the case until April 8, 1997, he said.

Regulatory reform is a key part of the solution to shipment problems that have plagued Canada's grain transportation system in recent years, CP Rail System assistant vice president of grain Ray Foot told delegates.
A system that forces accountability may ensure enhanced performance, he added.
Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale on Tuesday reiterated his committment to drafting legislation that rewards prompt shipment and penalizes certain delays.
Foot also called for reduced fuel taxes, stating that in certain cases the tax as much as doubles the fuel costs of a train run.
Dedicated train runs such as last summer's from Saskatchewan and Manitoba hauling oats to General Mills' facilities in Minneapolis may be another solution, he said.
Another pilot project saw the use of new, higher capacity hopper cars to Vancouver export terminal elevators where train turn around times were improved by 50 percent, Foot added.
CP Rail System spent C$175 million to buy 1,400 new high capacity covered hopper cars, he said.
